strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea of using a neural operator to predict the GMsFEM basis subspace rather than individual basis functions, addressing a real computational bottleneck (solving local spectral eigenproblems) in a well-established multiscale numerical method.

The proposed subspace alignment loss (and its projection-regularized variant) is grounded in principal-angle/Grassmannian subspace geometry and empirically outperforms a naive sign-invariant L2 loss on individual basis functions across all tested configurations (both PDEs, both forcing terms, both Nbf values), giving a consistent picture of improvement.

Strong quantitative gains are demonstrated: ~50x-60x speedup in basis-function generation relative to classical GMsFEM offline stage, and up to 1.7-1.8x error reduction relative to a standalone neural operator, with especially compelling out-of-distribution robustness (standalone NO errors exceeding 200%-2000% under distribution shift in forcing term, while GMsFEM-NO remains stable because it is agnostic to right-hand side/boundary conditions).
Reasonably thorough documentation of architectures, hyperparameter grids, and training protocols in the appendix, aiding reproducibility of the reported numbers even without released code.

The method cleanly separates offline (basis prediction) and online (coarse system solve) stages, preserving the interpretability and physics-consistency of GMsFEM while injecting NO speed only where it is expensive.
weaknesses: Experimental scope is narrow and small-scale: only a 100x100 fine grid with a 5x5 coarse grid (36 subdomains) on the unit square with Dirichlet BCs; no results at larger/finer resolutions or more complex geometries are given, making it hard to assess whether the 60x speedup and accuracy gains persist at realistic multiscale problem sizes.

No error bars, confidence intervals, or repeated runs are reported (explicitly acknowledged by the authors), so the reported improvements (e.g., GMsFEM-NO marginally beating GMsFEM itself in Table 2, or the loss-function comparisons in Table 1) cannot be judged for statistical robustness; some improvements are quite small (e.g., 2.49% vs 2.39% L2) and could plausibly fall within run-to-run variance.

The claim that GMsFEM-NO outperforms the GMsFEM basis functions it was trained to approximate is counterintuitive and only explained qualitatively ("redundancy reduction"), without rigorous analysis or ablation isolating this effect; this weakens confidence in an otherwise notable claim.

Reported speedup (Table 3) only covers the offline basis-generation inference cost, not amortized NO training time (20-150 minutes per NO, with 3 NOs per configuration); a full cost-benefit comparison against GMsFEM's offline cost, including amortization break-even analysis, is missing.

The subspace alignment loss closely resembles established principal-angle/chordal-distance metrics from the Grassmannian subspace-learning literature; the paper does not clearly situate its loss relative to this prior body of work, somewhat overstating novelty.

The approach requires training three separate NOs per subdomain geometry (full/half/corner) with per-configuration hyperparameter tuning (different mode counts, layers, batch sizes per loss/domain/dataset in the appendix tables), which suggests limited plug-and-play generality and considerable engineering/tuning overhead not fully reflected in the headline efficiency claims.

No code or data are released at submission (promised only upon acceptance), and the paper does not compare directly and empirically against the most closely related prior work (Spiridonov et al. 2025) as a baseline, despite discussing it as the nearest related approach.

The study is restricted to two time-independent, Dirichlet-only PDE benchmarks on structured grids, and the authors themselves note the architecture cannot handle irregular domains, limiting practical significance for the stated real-world applications (reservoir modeling, composite materials, subsurface flow).

strengths: The core idea—training a neural operator to predict a low-dimensional GMsFEM basis subspace rather than individual eigenfunctions—is a reasonable and moderately novel combination of classical multiscale FEM theory with neural operators.

The proposed subspace alignment loss (SAL) elegantly handles the non-uniqueness (sign/rotation) of basis functions by comparing orthonormalized subspaces via Frobenius-norm overlap, which is a sensible improvement over a naive per-basis-function L2 loss.
The experiments demonstrate a large (50-60x) speedup in basis-function generation relative to classical GMsFEM, which is the paper's most convincing quantitative result.

The out-of-distribution experiment (Table 5) convincingly illustrates a real practical limitation of standalone neural operators (catastrophic failure under distribution shift in forcing terms) and a genuine advantage of the proposed hybrid approach.
Reasonably detailed hyperparameter/training documentation is provided in the appendix, aiding reproducibility of the reported configurations.
weaknesses: There is a clear discrepancy between the abstract's headline claim ('cuts solution error by approximately 60% compared with standalone NOs') and the actual numbers in Table 4, where the observed error reductions range from about 31% to 42%—nowhere close to 60%. This overstatement of the central quantitative claim is a serious concern for a paper whose main contribution rests on this comparison.

All experiments use a single, small problem setting (100x100 fine grid, fixed 5x5 coarse grid, single contrast range [1,9600]); there is no study of how performance scales with grid resolution, coarse-grid size, or higher contrast, undermining claims of general applicability to 'multiscale PDE solving.'

No error bars, confidence intervals, or repeated-trial statistics are reported anywhere (explicitly acknowledged by the authors), making it impossible to assess whether the reported improvements (e.g., SAL vs RBFL2, GMsFEM-NO vs GMsFEM) are statistically meaningful or within noise, especially since some differences (e.g., Diffusion (7), Nbf=8: 1.06% vs 1.06%) are essentially negligible.

The claim that GMsFEM-NO outperforms the GMsFEM basis functions it was trained to approximate (Table 2) is counter-intuitive and only explained qualitatively/heuristically ('reduces redundancies'); no rigorous analysis or ablation is given to substantiate this surprising result, raising concerns about whether the comparison setup (e.g., evaluation metric coupling) is fully fair.

The comparison between the proposed method (3 specialized NOs, one per subdomain type, extensively hyperparameter-tuned per configuration) and the standalone baseline NO (a single network with a more limited hyperparameter search and different optimizer/training protocol) is not clearly matched in model capacity or tuning effort, making the 'NO vs GMsFEM-NO' comparison (Section 3.4) potentially unfair to the baseline.

The method is restricted to structured grids, Dirichlet BCs, and only two PDE types, which the authors acknowledge but which substantially limits the significance/generality of the contribution relative to real-world multiscale applications (e.g., reservoir modeling, composite materials) mentioned as motivation.

No code or data is released at submission time, and given the complexity of the pipeline (rotation normalization, three separate networks per subdomain type, multiple loss variants), independent reproduction would be difficult without released artifacts.

The technical contribution is somewhat incremental: it largely combines existing tools (GMsFEM, FFNO, subspace/Grassmannian alignment losses common in representation learning) without deep theoretical analysis of why/when the subspace loss should outperform pointwise losses, or convergence/error guarantees connecting the learned subspace quality to the final PDE solution accuracy.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel idea: instead of training a neural operator to predict individual GMsFEM basis functions (which are sensitive to sign/rotation ambiguities), the paper proposes learning the underlying low-dimensional subspace via a subspace-alignment loss (SAL/SAL-PR), which is a sensible and well-motivated design choice grounded in the non-uniqueness of eigenbasis representations.

The hybrid GMsFEM-NO approach cleverly retains the structural rigor/interpretability of multiscale finite elements (projection via restriction matrix R, online-stage solve) while replacing the expensive offline eigenproblem with fast NO inference, achieving ~50-60x speedup in basis generation with comparable or slightly better accuracy than classical GMsFEM.

Demonstrates a clear and practically important advantage over standalone NOs: independence from forcing terms/boundary conditions, with dramatic (>200%) error blowup for standalone NOs under out-of-distribution forcing versus stable performance for GMsFEM-NO — a compelling argument for the hybrid design.

Evaluated on two distinct PDE types (linear elliptic diffusion and nonlinear steady-state Richards equation) with high contrast coefficients (up to 9600x), and ablates loss function choice (RBFL2 vs SAL vs SAL-PR) and number of basis functions (4 vs 8), providing a reasonably thorough set of comparisons for the claims made.

Good reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameter grids and training configurations for all experiments are given in the appendix, and the checklist is largely filled out with concrete justifications.
weaknesses: Experiments are conducted at a fairly small scale: 100x100 fine grid, only a 5x5 coarse grid (36 subdomains) — it is unclear how the method scales to finer resolutions, more coarse cells, or 3D domains, and this limits confidence in the significance of the reported speedups/accuracy gains for realistic large-scale applications.

No error bars, confidence intervals, or repeated-seed statistics are reported anywhere in the paper (explicitly acknowledged in the checklist); given some of the reported gains are quite small (e.g., Diffusion Nbf=8 case shows virtually identical L2 between RBFL2 and SAL, 1.06% vs 1.06%), it's hard to assess whether the improvements are statistically meaningful or within noise.

The 'standalone NO vs GMsFEM-NO' baseline comparison (Table 4) uses a differently configured/trained NO (different optimizer - Lion vs AdamW, different learning rate schedule, different training budget) than the FFNOs used inside GMsFEM-NO, raising concerns about whether the comparison is fully controlled/fair rather than confounded by training-protocol differences.

The pipeline requires training three separate NOs per PDE/right-hand-side/basis-count combination (one per subdomain type: full/half/corner), plus manual rotation-based preprocessing to normalize subdomain orientation — this adds considerable engineering complexity and a combinatorial number of models to train/maintain, which is not clearly discussed as a cost/limitation relative to the claimed 'practical solver' framing.

The related prior work (Spiridonov et al. 2025, using an FC network for one additional basis function) is only discussed qualitatively; no direct empirical comparison against this or any other existing hybrid multiscale-ML baseline is provided, weakening the positioning of the contribution relative to the closest prior art.

Scope is limited to time-independent equations with Dirichlet boundary conditions on structured grids only, as acknowledged in the limitations, which considerably narrows the claimed applicability to 'heterogeneous PDEs' and 'multiscale PDE solving' in general.

Data generation process for the heterogeneous coefficient fields (e.g., layered structure shown in Fig. 4a) is not clearly described in terms of diversity/coverage, making it hard to judge how representative the 1000-sample dataset is of realistic high-contrast media or how well conclusions would generalize to different heterogeneity structures (e.g., channelized/composite geometries).

strengths: Novel and well-motivated hybrid framework (GMsFEM-NO) that targets a real bottleneck (costly local eigenproblems in the GMsFEM offline stage) while preserving the numerical-analysis foundation of GMsFEM at inference time.

The proposed subspace alignment loss (SAL) is grounded in Grassmannian geometry (Appendix C), giving a principled reason to prefer subspace-level training over pointwise basis-function regression, and the paper explicitly derives the connection to principal angles/projection distances.

Extensive empirical validation spanning 2D/3D, linear diffusion and nonlinear Richards equations, multiple grid resolutions (up to 100^3 in 3D), forcing-term variability, mixed boundary conditions, and a time-dependent heat equation.

Strong and diverse baseline comparisons: standalone SOTA NOs (F-FNO, GNOT, Transolver++), reduced-order/intrusive methods (POD, DeepONet/FFNO bases, DeepPOD, PCANet, kernel methods), giving a reasonably comprehensive picture of where the method sits relative to prior art.

Demonstrated practically useful properties: right-hand-side independence/OOD robustness, data efficiency relative to F-FNO, and resolution invariance (train on coarse grid, evaluate on finer grid) with reasonable accuracy retention.
Reported >60x speedup in basis generation with a computational breakeven analysis (though the analysis itself has some presentation issues, see weaknesses).
weaknesses: The theoretical error bound linking subspace alignment loss to actual solution error (Appendix C, Eq. 10) is left incomplete; the authors themselves state that estimating this bound rigorously (especially in the required energy norm) 'needs to be addressed in the future,' which weakens the claimed 'rigorous numerical analysis' foundation touted in the abstract.

Performance advantages are inconsistent across configurations: for Nbf=4 the method actually underperforms the standalone NO (Appendix J), and in the intrusive-baseline comparison (Appendix G, Fig. 5) DeepPOD with more (20-30) dense basis functions matches or beats GMsFEM-NO's 8 localized basis functions, suggesting the reported superiority is somewhat basis-count- and setting-dependent rather than universal.

The out-of-distribution comparison against standalone NOs (Table 13) is somewhat of a strawman, since standard NOs are trained for a fixed forcing term and never intended to generalize across right-hand sides without retraining; this is an inherent structural property rather than a fully fair apples-to-apples evaluation.

No uncertainty quantification (error bars, variance across seeds/runs) is reported for any L2/H1 numbers, and many reported improvements (e.g., 1.72% vs 1.82%) are small, making it hard to assess statistical significance of the claimed gains over GMsFEM and over SAL vs SAL-PR.

The method requires training separate NOs per local-domain geometric type (3 in 2D, 4 in 3D) with per-type architecture/hyperparameter tuning, adding substantial engineering overhead and complicating extension to irregular/unstructured meshes, which is explicitly left as future work, limiting applicability to realistic geometries.

The breakeven/cost analysis in Appendix N produces negative breakeven sample counts in all configurations, which is confusingly presented and not clearly explained; if the intended meaning is that the method is favorable even for very small numbers of inference queries, this should be clarified, and additional cases where the crossover might be unfavorable (e.g., very small numbers of test coefficients) are not explored.

Novelty relative to the closest related work (Spiridonov et al. 2025, which uses NNs to predict GMsFEM basis functions) is somewhat incremental, being mainly a change in architecture (predicting the full basis subspace via an NO rather than one supplementary function via an MLP) plus the new loss; the conceptual leap beyond existing hybrid multiscale-ML literature could be argued to be moderate rather than transformative.

Dataset sizes are modest, particularly for the largest 3D case (100x100x100, only 150 train/50 test samples), which may limit the robustness of conclusions drawn for large-scale settings that the paper positions as a key motivation.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated problem: accelerating the costly offline eigenproblem stage of GMsFEM while retaining its numerical-analysis guarantees, rather than replacing the whole solver with a black-box NO.

The subspace alignment loss (SAL) is a reasonable design choice with some theoretical grounding, being shown to equal (a scaled) Grassmannian distance between predicted and target subspaces, and an (incomplete but suggestive) error bound is sketched in Appendix C.

Fairly extensive empirical evaluation across 2D/3D, linear diffusion and nonlinear Richards equations, multiple grid resolutions, and additional experiments on a time-dependent heat equation and mixed boundary conditions.

Comparisons against a reasonably broad set of baselines (F-FNO, GNOT, Transolver++, POD/DeepPOD/PCANet/Kernel methods), showing the subspace/basis-learning strategy is generally more data-efficient and avoids catastrophic failure on out-of-distribution forcing terms compared to standalone NOs.
Demonstrated resolution invariance (train on coarse grid, evaluate on finer grid) and substantial (60x+) reduction in basis-generation wall-clock time versus classical GMsFEM.
weaknesses: The cost-benefit/breakeven analysis in Appendix N reports negative breakeven sample counts (e.g., x = -3270, -159) with no explanation of what a negative value means; given that Tdata (based on 800 traditional GMsFEM runs) plus Ttrain should only increase the number of inference samples needed to amortize cost relative to generating the training set alone, a negative value appears to indicate either a sign/formula error or an unexplained inconsistency, undermining confidence in the paper's central efficiency claims for realistic deployment.

Novelty relative to cited closely related work (Spiridonov et al. 2025; Kröpfl et al. 2022/2025) is somewhat incremental: the core idea of training a network to predict multiscale/GMsFEM basis functions is not new, and the main claimed novelty is restricted to the loss function formulation (subspace alignment vs. pointwise L2).

The theoretical analysis in Appendix C explicitly acknowledges it does not rigorously connect SAL to solution error in the relevant (energy) norm, stating that "these questions need to be addressed in the future," so the paper's claim of a solution grounded in "rigorous numerical analysis" is only partially substantiated.

Mixed empirical results undercut the superiority narrative: for Nbf = 4, GMsFEM-NO underperforms the standalone NO and was abandoned without further investigation; in Table 8, F-FNO with the full training set actually outperforms GMsFEM-NO on the Diffusion-8 case; and in the intrusive-baseline comparison (Appendix G/Fig. 5), DeepPOD with ~20-30 (dense) basis functions matches or beats GMsFEM-NO with 8 (sparse) basis functions, suggesting the proposed method's advantage is more nuanced/basis-count-dependent than the abstract/conclusion imply.

Experiments are restricted to structured, box-shaped domains and simple KLE-generated synthetic coefficient fields; the paper itself lists extension to irregular/unstructured meshes as future work, which is a substantial limitation given GMsFEM's traditional applicability to complex geometries.

No reporting of variance/uncertainty across multiple training runs or random seeds, making it hard to assess whether reported small accuracy differences (e.g., 1.05% vs 1.13%) are statistically meaningful or within noise.

The out-of-distribution failure numbers for the standalone NO baseline (up to 6554% relative error in Table 13) seem implausibly extreme and are not critically discussed; this raises a question of whether the baseline NO was handicapped (e.g., insufficiently diverse right-hand side training data) rather than inherently incapable, which would inflate the apparent advantage of GMsFEM-NO.

The paper's writing relegates almost all key technical and experimental substance (loss derivations, baseline details, OOD results, time/breakeven analysis, additional PDEs) to a very long appendix, leaving the main text somewhat thin on critical discussion of limitations and making it hard to evaluate the work's core claims without extensive appendix cross-referencing.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically important bottleneck: the expensive local eigenproblem solves in the offline stage of GMsFEM, and proposes a principled way to accelerate it with neural operators while retaining the underlying numerical-analysis structure of GMsFEM.

The subspace-informed loss (Grassmannian/subspace alignment loss, with a projection-regularization variant) is theoretically motivated; Appendix C rigorously connects the proposed loss to the classical Grassmannian distance between subspaces, giving the method a sound geometric justification beyond simple L2 regression on individual eigenfunctions.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: 2D and 3D diffusion and nonlinear Richards' equation, multiple grid/coarse-mesh sizes, ablations over loss functions (RBFL2 vs SAL vs SAL-PR), Nbf=4 vs 8, comparisons against several categories of baselines (POD, DeepONet/FFNO-based intrusive POD, PCANet, kernel methods, DeepPOD, and SOTA standalone NOs F-FNO/GNOT/Transolver++), resolution-invariance experiments, out-of-distribution forcing-term tests, time-dependent and mixed-boundary-condition extensions, and a detailed timing/breakeven analysis.

Demonstrates a clear practical advantage over standalone NOs: robustness to unseen forcing terms (standalone NO errors exceeding 100-1000% OOD vs. stable performance for GMsFEM-NO), improved data efficiency, and >60x speedup in basis generation compared to classical GMsFEM while nearly matching its accuracy.

The paper is transparent about limitations, including an unresolved theoretical gap linking subspace angle to solution error, restriction to structured grids, and reporting cases (e.g., DeepPOD with more basis functions, Nbf=4 configuration) where the proposed method's advantage narrows or disappears, which strengthens the credibility of the empirical claims.
Reasonable reproducibility support: extensive appendices detailing architecture/hyperparameter grids, dataset generation (KLE fields), and promised code release.
weaknesses: Core technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the main contributions are (1) applying an existing numerical method (GMsFEM) plus an existing NO architecture (F-FNO) and (2) a subspace-alignment loss based on a known Grassmannian distance concept; there is limited fundamentally new architectural or algorithmic innovation, and a closely related prior work (Spiridonov et al. 2025) already explored NN-predicted GMsFEM basis functions.

The appendix comparison with DeepPOD undercuts the paper's overall superiority narrative: DeepPOD with ~20-30 dense basis functions matches or outperforms GMsFEM-NO with only 8 localized basis functions, suggesting the advantage of GMsFEM-NO may be more about efficiency/localization than absolute accuracy, and this nuance is not adequately reflected in the main text/abstract claims.

The method requires training a separate specialized NO for each geometric domain type (3 types in 2D, 4 in 3D), which adds non-trivial engineering complexity and does not naturally generalize to irregular/unstructured domains — explicitly acknowledged as a limitation but not yet addressed even partially in this work.

Experiments remain at relatively modest scale (up to 250×250 in 2D and 100^3 in 3D, with only 150 training/50 test samples for the largest 3D case), leaving open how the approach scales to truly large, industrial-scale heterogeneous domains.
Performance degrades substantially for Nbf=4 (worse than a standalone NO), indicating sensitivity to the number of basis functions and limiting the generality of the claimed benefits.

The theoretical error bound in Appendix C is incomplete — the authors themselves note that translating subspace/principal-angle closeness into a rigorous bound on final solution error remains unresolved, which weakens the abstract's claim of "retaining foundation in rigorous numerical analysis."
All experiments use synthetic KLE-generated coefficient fields; no validation on real-world heterogeneous/geological data is provided, limiting evidence of practical applicability.

The breakeven/timing analysis in Appendix N is presented somewhat confusingly (negative "x" values for breakeven sample counts), and while it shows the method is beneficial in tested regimes, sequential vs. parallel training cost comparisons could be clearer and more systematically justified.
